1970 GTO Judge 4-Speed Is Rarer Than Hen's Teeth, Carries Scarce Factory Option for Everyone To See
37 photos
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi
Typically, enthusiasts picture Pontiac’s muscle car’s muscle car drenched in screaming Carousel Red or Orbit Orange. One Maryland couple decided to break that stereotype into smithereens with their Palomino Copper 1970 hardtop. With a 4-speed behind the Ram Air 400, because that’s how a Judge strikes his gavel after a ruling.
Eric and Laura O'Dell of Sykesville, Maryland, couldn’t not have found a more subtle way to make the loudest statement at any car meet. Their muscle car (“real + rare”) will not draw attention with bright colors, but it doesn’t need a colorful fluff of feathers to stand out.
Up front, the flexible Endura urethane bumper frames quad exposed round headlamps and a black-textured split grille carrying the classic GTO badge. A black vanity plate spells out “The Judge” immediately below the beak, while dual functional hood scoops display "Ram Air" callouts beside the hood-mounted tachometer.
Swooping multi-colored 1970 eyebrow stripes trace the wheel arches above bright yellow “Judge” fender decals, leading back to a body-colored pedestal airfoil, quad chrome exhaust tips, and trim-ring-free Rally II wheels wrapped in Firestone Wide Oval G70-14 tires. Its classy, tasteful, elegant, sublime, and impeccable. If it were to attend a beauty pageant, it wouldn’t win the crown; it would be the one awarding it.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Inside, Saddle vinyl Strato-bucket seats with headrests and shoulder harnesses flank a matching center console housing the signature Hurst T-handle 4-speed shifter. Three deep gauge pods punctuate the simulated woodgrain instrument panel alongside a three-spoke steering wheel, AM pushbutton radio, and a glovebox Judge emblem.
Under the hood, a freshly detailed Pontiac Metallic Blue 400-cubic-inch V8 with chrome valve covers wears its Ram Air foam pan seal, playfully cradling two plush tigers while a third stuffed feline peeks from the open trunk beside a gavel, Matchbox Judge, period brochures, and documentation binder.
That open three-ring binder and the reproduced Pontiac window sticker affixed to the rear quarter glass reveal the hardtop’s genuine provenance. It’s a true 242 GTO Hardtop Coupe, put together at General Motors’ Baltimore, Maryland assembly plant. Window sticker data confirms Pontiac shipped it new to Miller Pontiac-GMC Inc. in St. Cloud, Minnesota, before it eventually returned to its home state.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Tracing the car’s online footprint uncovers no auction-flip listings or salvage history, pointing instead to steady enthusiast stewardship. Eric and Laura O'Dell have full bragging rights about their spectacular muscle car – and spectacular is not figuratively used here. This car has earned a Special Ward in the Standard of excellence category at the 2025 Carlisle Nationals (the GM Nationals, obviously, if it needs clarification).
As revered as it is today, the Pontiac GTO Judge actually didn’t always get the honors the name would imply. Starting from a $3,267 base price plus an $88 freight charge to Minnesota for a $3,355 sub-total, the original buyer checked code WT1 for The Judge package (at $337.02) and the M20 4-speed manual (a hefty $184.80).
Adding variable-ratio power steering at $105.32, the hood-mounted tachometer at $63.19, Soft-Ray tinted glass at $36.86, an electric clock at $18.96, wheel-opening moldings at $15.80, a remote mirror at $10.53, and heavy-duty springs and shocks at $4.21, plus power brakes, console, and AM radio, pushed the final tally to $4,249.66.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi That substantial bottom line was actually the exact opposite of what Pontiac originally intended when it hatched The Judge for 1969. By late 1968, the GTO that invented the muscle car segment was losing showroom ground to Plymouth’s stripped-down, budget-priced Road Runner and Chevrolet’s Chevelle SS 396.
John DeLorean and marketing ace Jim Wangers initially sketched a bare-bones street fighter dubbed the GTO E/T before DeLorean rejected the name and lifted The Judge from Flip Wilson’s recurring Laugh-In comedy skit, inadvertently creating the loudest, priciest GTO in history.
Pontiac kept The Judge on the docket for just three model years, from 1969 through early 1971, halting new orders on March 1, 1971 as insurance surcharges and tightening emissions squeezed Detroit. Across that brief run, Pontiac built exactly 11,004 Judges, split between 10,711 hardtop coupes and only 293 convertibles.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Volume peaked immediately in 1969 at 6,833 cars, comprising 6,725 hardtops and 108 soft-tops, before dropping sharply in 1970 to 3,797 units, divided between 3,629 hardtops and 168 ragtops, and collapsing in 1971 to 374 examples: 357 hardtops and 17 droptops.
Breaking down the 1970 Judge model year by engine and transmission shows just how selective buyers were during muscle’s high-water mark. Of the 3,797 Judges built for 1970, ] 3,383 left the factory with the standard 400-cubic-inch Ram Air III V8.
Within that Ram Air III group, 1,831 WS-code cars received the M20 wide-ratio 4-speed manual like the O'Dell’s example, 425 WS builds took the M21 close-ratio 4-speed, 124 WS cars kept the heavy-duty M13 3-speed stick, and 1,003 YZ-code Judges paired the engine with the M40 Turbo Hydra-Matic 400, also a 3-speed, but automatic .
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Pontiac produced 397 Ram Air IV Judges for 1970, 325 WW-code cars backed by the M21 close-ratio 4-speed and 72 XP-code examples shifting through the M40 automatic. Late in the model year, Pontiac also slipped its big-inch 455 into the Judge option list, producing only 17 YA- and YC-code cars—14 hardtops and 3 convertibles—every single one equipped with the M40 automatic.
Factor in the owner’s estimate that roughly 18 hardtops wore Palomino Copper metallic, and this Maryland M20 coupe sits deep in blue-chip unicorn territory. The walkaround video (courtesy of Don Shinobi’s YouTube channel) is a brief deposition in favor of the car’s undeniable presence.
In a sense, it’s like the perfect tie for a gentleman’s suit: it’s so discrete, no on remembers it after a face-to-face meeting. But it makes all the difference in the world, complementing the owner to the fullest.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Standard for 1969 and 1970, the 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) L74 Ram Air III combined a 4.12-inch bore, 3.75-inch stroke, four-bolt-mains iron block, 10.5:1 compression, Rochester Quadrajet four-barrel carburetor, high-flow iron exhaust manifolds, and a 288/302-degree manual-transmission camshaft to generate 366 hp (371 PS) at 5,100 rpm and 445 lb-ft (603 Nm) at 3,600 rpm.
The optional Ram Air IV added round-port heads, a high-rise aluminum intake, 308/320-degree cam, and header-like manifolds, conservatively rated at 370 hp (375 PS) at 5,500 rpm and 445 lb-ft (603 Nm) at 3,900 rpm.
When GM lifted its mid-size engine displacement ceiling for 1970, Pontiac unleashed the 455-cubic-inch (7.5-liter) V8 good for 360 hp (365 PS) at 4,300 rpm alongside an earth-moving 500 lb-ft (678 Nm) of torque at 2,700 rpm. For 1971, GM mandated lower compression for unleaded fuel, retiring both Ram Air 400s in favor of the sole 455 H.O.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Despite dropping to 8.4:1 compression, its round-port heads and aluminum intake still produced 335 hp (340 PS) gross hp at 4,800 rpm and 480 lb-ft (651 Nm) at 3,600 rpm. Period magazine road tests confirmed that Pontiac’s paperwork underplayed what these engines could do when hooked to proper gearing.
In April 1969, Speed and Supercars hustled a Ram Air III Judge down the quarter-mile in 13.88 seconds at 102.6 mph (165.1 kph), while Car Life ran a 4-speed 400 Ram Air GTO in 14.60 seconds at 99.55 mph (160.2 kph). Car Life timed a 1969 Ram Air IV Judge from 0 to 60 mph in 6.2 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 14.45 seconds at 97.8 mph (157.4 kph), reaching 124 mph (200 kph), before Super Stock & Drag Illustrated blasted a 1970 Ram Air IV Judge to 13.60 seconds at 104.5 mph (168.2 kph).
Torque-rich 455 models proved slightly less frantic at the strip yet far friendlier in everyday traffic. Testing an automatic 1970 GTO 455 directly against the 4-speed Ram Air 400, Car Life recorded 14.76 seconds at 95.94 mph (154.4 kph) while returning 12 mpg versus the peaky 400’s dismal 8 mpg.
Photo: YouTube/Don Shinobi Car and Driver logged 15.0 seconds at 96.5 mph (155.3 kph) and a 120 mph (193 kph) estimated top speed in its January 1970 GTO 455 test. By October 1970, Motor Trend clocked the lower-compression 1971 455 H.O. through the quarter-mile in 14.90 seconds at 95 mph (152.9 kph), with other period runs dipping into the mid-14s and low-6-second 0-to-60 mph sprints.
That firepower was critical for a 1970 Judge that had rolled onto the streets during the fiercest horsepower war Detroit ever waged. Inside General Motors alone, Pontiac battled Chevrolet’s 450-hp Chevelle SS 454 LS6, Buick’s torque-laden GS 455 Stage 1 and GSX, and Oldsmobile’s refined 4-4-2 W-30.
Across town, Chrysler answered with 440 Six-Pack and 426 Hemi versions of the Plymouth Road Runner, Plymouth GTX, Dodge Super Bee, and Dodge Charger R/T, while Ford fielded the Torino Cobra 429 Super Cobra Jet, Mercury counterpunched with the Cyclone Spoiler, and AMC joined the fray with its brash Rebel The Machine.
More than half a century after leaving Baltimore for a Minnesota showroom, Eric and Laura O'Dell’s Palomino Copper hardtop proves that a muscle car does not need neon paint to command respect. Preserved with its factory Ram Air III punch, M20 4-speed cogbox, and full PHS paper trail, this understated 1970 Judge stands as a rolling reminder of the year Detroit threw subtlety out the window—even when one clever buyer quietly ordered his outlaw in metallic copper.

Bugatti Nearly Replaced the Chiron With an Electric SUV, Mate Rimac Fought Against It
10 photos
Photo: colekessel | Instagram
Bugatti was inches away from replacing the Chiron with an electric SUV in 2020. The Volkswagen Group was racing, full speed ahead, toward an all-electric future, and the EV seemed the right way at the time. They asked for the help of the Rimac founder, Mate Rimac, to build it, and he fought against the idea with everything he had.
One day, Mate Rimac got an email from the head of strategy at Volkswagen inviting him to Germany to talk about Bugatti. It was a time when Bugatti was desperately trying to figure out what would make a great successor or replacement.
At the time, Stephan Winkelmann served as President of Bugatti Automobiles, later taking on the additional role of Lamborghini CEO in late 2020 until the Bugatti Rimac joint venture formed in November 2021. Winklemann was among the executives who championed the idea of a four-door electric Bugatti and pushed toward an all-electric brand.
The plan was to launch an electric Bugatti, with four seats and high ground clearance, and they wanted the platform of the Nevera for it. So Mate Rimac’s team had to rearrange the architecture to fit the new Bugatti. A new platform would have cost billions, and the auto group did not have that much money.
Photo: spdesignsest | Instagram Furthermore, even though the group is famous for sharing platforms across brands, none of them could have handled the size, weight, and extreme power targets of a Bugatti electric SUV . The project never got the green light, and work did not even start. The business case simply did not make financial sense.
Mate Rimac proposed to the Volkswagen Group executives that they would develop and build a successor for the outgoing Chiron, and Bugatti would only have to sell it. The head of strategy at Volkswagen suddenly asked him: " Why don't you take over the company? "
Mate never took that awkward question seriously and laughed it off until he got a phone call months later. He eventually said yes, and here he was, the founder of a hypercar company from Croatia becoming the CEO of Bugatti.
Two and a half years later, on a call with 90 people, 85 from Volkswagen and five from Rimac Automobili, he talked about the future of Bugatti. Volkswagen kept insisting on an electric SUV , while Mate fought against the idea with everything he had, he admitted in an interview with Classic Driver, even though he did not know anything about building cars with internal combustion engines.
Photo: spdesignsest | Instagram The Rimac Nevera , the model they had in development at the time, was this limited-run, mind-blowing hypercar, powered by four independent liquid-cooled permanent-magnet motors, one for each wheel.
The quad-motor setup puts to the ground a massive 1,888 horsepower (1,914 metric horsepower) and 1,726 pound-feet (2,340 Newton meters) of torque. That was enough to make it rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 1.74 seconds and all the way to a top speed of 258 mph (412 kph).
The Nevera R was even more impressive. It was factory-rated at 2,078 horsepower (2,107 metric horsepower) and the same amount of torque for a run from 0 to 60 mph in just 1.66 seconds and a top speed of 268 mph (431 kph).
Volkswagen was well aware that they couldn’t put that in an SUV , but they wanted the closest thing to it. " No can do ," Rimac told them. His refusal made way for the Bugatti Tourbillon . By the time the project started, he was already the CEO of Bugatti, and he could lead the development, engineering, and prototype testing.
Photo: Bugatti Instead of the electric powertrain that the Volkswagen Group originally wanted, he came up with the Cosworth-developed 8.3-liter V16 with naturally aspirated firepower, built to replace the 8.0-liter W16 in both the Veyron and the Chiron. The V16 works alongside two electric motors up front and one driving the rear wheels.
The setup pumps out 1,775 horsepower (1,800 metric horsepower) and 1,696 pound-feet (2,300 Newton meters) of torque. The Tourbillon flashes from 0 to 60 mph in 1.9 seconds and reaches a top speed of 276 mph (445 kph) with the Speed Key engaged.
Just like the Rimac Nevera, the Tourbillon sits on an 800-volt electrical architecture, but while the Nevera is built around Rimac’s carbon fiber monocoque, the Tourbillon received a clean-sheet Bugatti T800 carbon monocoque.
The Bugatti Tourbillon was officially unveiled on June 20, 2024. Only 250 units would see the light of day, each starting at 3.8 million euros (nearly $4.2 million) before starting to check any option boxes and before taxes and fees. All of the 250 units had already been spoken for before the official unveiling.
Photo: Bugatti It is already 2026, and there is still no electric Bugatti on the market or in development, because the brand's clientele is not exactly ready to ditch the raw emotion, mechanical drama, and unmistakable sound of a multi-cylinder combustion engine.
In the meantime, the auto group learned from others’ mistakes. They saw what Ferrari had to deal with when it launched the Purosangue and then, in 2026, the backlash that the Italians had to deal with when they launched their first EV, the Luce.

New 2027 KGM Rexton Realistically Imagined, Just Don’t Call It a SsangYong Anymore
6 photos
Photo: Kolesa
SsangYong officially changed its corporate name to KG Mobility (KGM) in 2023, and from 2023 to 2025, it gradually changed the names of its models in individual markets. As a result, the Rexton is now a KGM-branded product, and it’s obviously not the only one.
We will focus on this exact model in this story because it is about to be completely renewed. And it will be a much deserved makeover, because the second generation, aka the current one, is on the aging side of things. Production started in 2017, and the model was also marketed as a Mahindra (Alturas G4) at one point in India.
It is related to the Musso pickup, comes to life in its homeland of South Korea, and is offered with gasoline and diesel engines, paired with manual and automatic transmissions. The current KGM Rexton measures 190.9 inches (4,850 mm) in length, 77.2 inches (1,960 mm) in width, and 71.9 inches (1,825 mm) in height, and has a 112.8 inches (2,865 mm) long wheelbase.
The third-generation is in the making as we speak, and we wouldn’t be surprised if it become a bit larger. The Korean company itself recently dropped a few teasers of the upcoming Rexton, previewing it from a few angles, and those images were used by Kolesa’s pixel master, Nikita Chuyko, to create these realistic renderings.
The grille somewhat reminds us of Jeep, and the back end kind of looks like a Range Rover. The exterior design is entirely new, and looks nothing like the one of the current KGM Rexton. The new one features pixelated headlights and daytime running lights that have been extended to the much smaller grille.
The front bumper is a lot smaller and much cleaner-looking, and sports new individual turn signals on the outer edges, and redesigned vents. The hood also looks completely different, though we can see some lines inspired by its predecessor on the front fenders. The lower parts of the doors and the side skirts are more aggressive, and in these CGIs, the new Rexton sports traditional door handles.
Photo: KGM On the sides, it features shorter windows, and has a roofline that is slightly arched toward the rear. The new taillights are vertical and much slimmer than before. The tailgate looks evolutionary, and the bumper much cleaner. It is also worth noting that the rear pillars are a lot thinner, so the rear three-quarter visibility has likely improved. The rendered new-gen KGM Rexton has black cladding on the lower parts of the body, and sits on new and bigger wheels.
The model’s overall design is definitely softer, and to be honest, not that bad. It is officially dubbed the KGM Rexton PHEV, and it is the first of its kind to pack a plug-in hybrid powertrain, as its name implies. The ladder-frame construction should be ditched in favor of a unibody, and rumor has it that it will be based on Chery’s T2X platform as part of a collaboration between the two brands.
If this is indeed the case, then the new Rexton will have nothing in common anymore with the next-gen KGM Musso pickup, which is expected to retain its ladder-frame bones. The Korean firm will drop more details on its upcoming Rexton toward the end of the year, and in January 2027, the model will launch in its homeland of South Korea.
We don’t need to remind you that it won’t make it to the United States, do we? After all, no KGM-branded products are being marketed over here, and the lineup includes models such as the Tivoli, Torres, Actyon, Rexton, and Musso, as well as several derivatives, in the UK, anyway, the KGM official website reveals.
Now, assuming that the all-new KGM Rexton will indeed look exactly like this rendered model, would you buy one if you could? Keep in mind that, as mentioned above, these digital illustrations are based on official teasers, so they are very realistic.

source_document.body:
Aerial view of the Cusi project area in Mexico. Credit: Silverco Mining.
By: Northern Miner Staff November 26, 2026
Silverco Mining (TSXV: SICO, US-OTC: SICOF) secured up to $15 million (C$21.3 million) in financing tied to concentrate sales from its newly restarted Cusi mine in Mexico, giving the company more room to fund the ramp-up of two underground operations through the first half of 2027. The stock rose.
The agreement, disclosed late Wednesday along with third-quarter results , follows Cusi’s first concentrate shipment on Nov. 16. Silverco aims to declare commercial production in the first half of next year at both Cusi in Chihuahua state and La Negra in Querétaro state, where a new underground fleet and tailings filtration plant are central to lifting mill throughput.
Shares of Silverco rose 6% to C$7.30 Thursday afternoon in Toronto, having earlier gained as much as 7.1%. That valued the company at about C$408 million ($287 million).
Silverco’s quarterly loss of 2¢ per share was narrower than the 8¢ average loss forecast by financial analysts, largely because costs came in below estimates.
“Our focus at La Negra remains on watching for unit costs to come down and grades to rise as productivity improvements are completed, translating into stronger margins, supplemented by the ramp-up at Cusi,” National Bank Capital Markets analyst Alex Terentiew wrote in a Thursday note. “Grade improvement remains central to our La Negra outlook.”
Nuevo deal
Higher throughput and recoveries at La Negra helped offset a silver grade of 49 grams per tonne, below Terentiew’s 55-gram forecast. Cash costs at the operation averaged about $54 per silver-equivalent oz., higher than a previous estimate of $50, the analyst said.
Silverco acquired La Negra in May through its all-share purchase of Nuevo Silver. In its first full quarter under Silverco, the mine processed 125,000 tonnes and produced 161,741 oz. of silver. Copper, lead and zinc brought total output to 348,578 silver-equivalent ounces. La Negra generated C$24.6 million in revenue and C$3.4 million in mine operating earnings. Silverco ended September with C$36.2 million in cash.
La Negra averaged about 1,360 tonnes per day over the quarter, just over half its 2,500-tonne design capacity.
The first unit of its new Epiroc fleet, an underground development drill, has arrived, and Silverco has awarded the civil works contract for the filtration plant. The company expects filtered tailings to ease the water-management constraint that limits mill throughput. It is targeting commissioning by the end of June.
Mine extension
Exploration could also extend the reach of the existing mine. On Tuesday, Silverco reported that a surface hole at Valenciana, about 650 metres northwest of La Negra’s mine infrastructure, cut 15.65 metres grading 322 grams silver per tonne from 224 metres depth. Underground drilling also extended mineralization down dip at the Valeria and Brecha deposits.
At Cusi, which had been on care and maintenance since September 2023, Silverco says the $19.2-million restart remains on budget. The company plans to hand over the refurbished Mal Paso mill to operations by the end of November and start extracting ore from its first stope at Promontorio late this quarter. Underground development continues at San Miguel as Silverco works toward the mill’s design rate of 1,200 tonnes per day.
Silverco can draw on the Cusi prepayment facility at its discretion, with each draw repayable over 24 months. The company says the two mines could deliver more than 4 million silver-equivalent oz. in 2027, based on their preliminary economic assessments.
